finding.claim: PUT /doc/<doc_id> overwrites any document body without an authorization check; can_edit() result is discarded, so any authenticated user can modify documents they do not own or edit (HIGH).
finding.source: Authenticated low-privilege caller reaching PUT /doc/<doc_id> with JSON {"body": ...}; doc_id must be known. Precondition: an auth layer populates g.user (not in this file).

trace.note: Route PUT /doc/<doc_id> registered with no auth or authz decorator
doc = DOCS[doc_id] loads any document by ID
can_edit(g.user, doc) called but return value discarded; no abort

finding.guards_checked: No before_request or permission middleware in docs.py; can_edit (docs.py:7-8) is a predicate that enforces nothing when its result is ignored; require_edit (docs.py:11-13) is correct but not called on this route; sibling update_title (docs.py:27) does call require_edit, giving 403 for the same user. If g.user is unset, line 19 raises AttributeError before the write (fails closed), so exploitation requires an auth layer that sets g.user, which was not verified.

verdict.guard_found: docs.py:7-8 can_edit is a bool predicate, and its result is discarded at docs.py:19 (bare call, no abort). docs.py:11-13 require_edit would abort(403), but it is not called on the PUT /doc/<doc_id> route at docs.py:16-21. No before_request, login_required, or g.user assignment exists in the directory (grep found none), so the auth layer the candidate assumed is absent from this codebase.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: the route at docs.py:16 has no authz decorator, can_edit at docs.py:19 returns a bool that is discarded, and docs.py:20 overwrites the body, while the sibling update_title at docs.py:27 correctly calls require_edit. The attacker is an authenticated low-privilege user, and no effective control blocks the write; the only caveat is that g.user is never assigned in this directory, so in this codebase the request would fail earlier with AttributeError at docs.py:19 (fail-closed), and the finding is real only once an auth layer populates g.user.

finding.claim: can_edit uses unvalidated comparisons: user in doc["editors"] becomes a substring match if editors is a string, and owner == user passes if both are None (LOW, conditional).
finding.source: Document records whose editors field is a string, or whose owner and g.user are both None. Data-population code is not in the repo.
finding.sink: Authorization decision in can_edit (docs.py:8), gating require_edit and the title route

trace.note: return doc["owner"] == user or user in doc["editors"]
require_edit(g.user, doc) on title route relies on can_edit

finding.guards_checked: Type validation of editors and owner is absent in this file; not verifiable without DOCS population code. Conditional, so LOW hardening note.

verdict.guard_found: No guard in docs.py blocks the comparison. require_edit (docs.py:11-13) does abort(403) on a False result, and the title route (docs.py:27) calls it correctly. The only remaining guard is the data population or auth middleware that sets g.user and DOCS, and neither is in the repo.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: docs.py:8 is the comparison, and docs.py:27 uses it through require_edit at docs.py:11-13. Whether the attacker can supply a string `editors` value or a None `g.user` depends on data-population and auth code that is not in this directory, so reachability cannot be decided here. Separately, docs.py:19 calls can_edit as a bare statement and discards the result, so update_doc at docs.py:17-21 performs no authorization check at all. That is a stronger issue than AUTH-2 and should be reported on its own.

finding.claim: Unhandled KeyError on DOCS[doc_id] and request.json["body"]/["title"] returns HTTP 500; on the title route an existing non-editable document returns 403 while a nonexistent ID returns 500, letting an authenticated user enumerate which document IDs exist (LOW).
finding.source: Authenticated caller supplying arbitrary doc_id values to PUT /doc/<doc_id>/title
finding.sink: DOCS[doc_id] lookup at docs.py:26 and the existence-dependent response

trace.note: doc = DOCS[doc_id] raises KeyError for unknown IDs, producing 500
require_edit returns 403 for existing documents the caller cannot edit
request.json["body"] KeyError or missing JSON gives 500

finding.guards_checked: No explicit 404 handling and no custom error handler in docs.py. Triage Check 8: non-actionable information disclosure, so LOW.

verdict.guard_found: none. There is no 404 handling or error handler in docs.py. The only check on the title route is require_edit (docs.py:11-13), which runs after the DOCS[doc_id] lookup at docs.py:26, so nonexistent IDs raise KeyError (500) and existing non-editable IDs get abort(403).
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: docs.py:26 raises KeyError for unknown IDs with no handler to map it to 404, while docs.py:27 returns 403 for existing documents the caller cannot edit, so an authenticated user can distinguish existing from nonexistent IDs. Impact is low, since it is information disclosure of document ID existence only. Separately, docs.py:19 calls can_edit(g.user, doc) as a bare statement with its result discarded, so update_doc at docs.py:17-21 has no authorization check at all; that is a more serious issue outside this candidate's scope and should be reported separately.
